component DispatchDeclaredDomain
export Executable
(* A generic declaration beside a plain one is chosen by their declared domains, in either order of writing. *)
trait Shape comprises { Circle, Square } end
object Circle extends Shape end
object Square extends Shape end
describeGenericFirst[\T extends Shape\](x: T): String = "generic"
describeGenericFirst(x: Circle): String = "circle"
describePlainFirst(x: Circle): String = "circle"
describePlainFirst[\T extends Shape\](x: T): String = "generic"
run(): () = do
    s: Shape = Circle
    assert(describeGenericFirst(Circle), "circle", "the plain declaration on Circle, written second, lies inside the generic declaration's domain, so a Circle takes it (Overloading Resolution)")
    assert(describeGenericFirst(Square), "generic", "only the generic declaration applies to a Square")
    assert(describeGenericFirst(s), "circle", "a Circle held as a Shape takes the plain declaration, dispatch reading the value")
    assert(describePlainFirst(Circle), "circle", "the plain declaration on Circle, written first, lies inside the generic declaration's domain, so a Circle takes it")
    assert(describePlainFirst(Square), "generic", "only the generic declaration applies to a Square")
    assert(describePlainFirst(s), "circle", "a Circle held as a Shape takes the plain declaration, dispatch reading the value")
    println("PASS")
  end
end

trait Marker[\X\] end

grab[\Y\](t: Sub[\Y\]): Marker[\Y\] = SubM[\Y\]

component XXXComprisesMeetGenericFunctions
export Executable
trait S[\X\] comprises { U[\X\], V[\X\] } end
trait T[\X\] comprises { V[\X\], W[\X\] } end
trait U[\X\] extends S[\X\] excludes W[\X\] end
trait V[\X\] extends { S[\X\], T[\X\] } end
trait W[\X\] extends T[\X\] end
object Vo extends V[\ZZ32\] end
tag[\X\](s: S[\X\]): ZZ32 = 1

tag[\X\](v: V[\X\]): ZZ32 = 3
run(): () = do
  s: S[\ZZ32\] = Vo
  assert(tag(s), 3, "tag of a V held as an S runs the declaration on V")
  println("PASS")
end
end

== explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:7-27

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

# The POPL 2019 examples, sorted for the test suite

## In short

- The paper and the talk hold 24 worked examples once the talk's builds that repeat a paper example are folded into it: 11 in group A, 4 in group B, 9 in group C.
- Of the 11 in group A, today's tree fails 4 on one path, and 2 more derived from group B and C examples fail too:
  - walk loads an object that inherits `m(x: Number)` with a body from two unrelated traits (p. 11:2; row 444's family);
  - walk loads `f(x: B): C` beside `f(x: C): B` with `object C extends B`, the talk's "NOT TYPE-SOUND" set (slide 4; a new row);
  - walk loads two generic `sort`s bounded by `A` and by `B` with no declaration at their meet (p. 11:5, slide 7; row 373);
  - the compiled path refuses the talk's opening `add` set, because the compiler prelude's `ZZ32` is an open trait (slide 2; a new row);
  - the paper's `ArrayList`/`List` triple fails on both paths, as its gated expected failures say (p. 11:13; rows 537 and 539);
  - derived: the paper's `sort` set with its meet written `P extends { A, B }` dies compiled (row 537), and the invariant core of the paper's `sort`/`merge` example fails on both paths (p. 11:7; one new compiled row, one walk row optional).
- Group B holds no new question for Pavol. The paper's two sets that rest on "C is the only subtype of both A and B" become valid in Fortress through `comprises` clauses, which the revival's Meet Rule reads as coverage; the union instance of `O.m(3, true)` is his decision for the bound; the No Duplicates wording is row 696.
- Group C waits on the `covariant` keyword (row 404), lower bounds on a method's type parameters, and the static return type carried to run time (phase 5).

## How the examples were run

- Each Fortress form is a test program in the form `tests-writing.md` gives: `component Name`, `export Executable`, the declarations shown, and `run(): () = do ... end` with the body shown. The scratch copies live in the tree's ignored `tmp/` and are not committed.
- Under walk: `bin/fortress walk P.fss`. Compiled: `bin/fortress compile P.fss`, then `bin/fortress run P`. Both with `FORTRESS_CACHES` pointing at a private copy of `default_repository/caches`, so the shared caches took no scratch entry.
- The existing tests named below were run through the harness: `harness-one.sh` on `XXXOverloadExistentialMeetWalk.fss` and `XXXGenericBesidePlainSameDomain.fss` printed `OK (2 tests)`; `junit.sh` with `ONE_JVM=1` on `OverloadExistentialMeetLink.test`, `XXXOverloadExistentialMeet.test`, `XXX2f.test`, `GenericInstanceUnfixedLink.test` and `XXXGenericInstanceUnfixed.test` printed `OK (5 tests)`, each `XXX` file as "Saw expected failure".
- In FGFV a method is called `e.m(e')`; the Fortress forms use top-level functions, which the revival overloads by the same rules (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading"). FGFV's classes become traits, or objects where the example needs a value.
- An overloading that breaks a rule is a static error on both paths: the rules are "checked statically" for the declarations, "whether or not these calls actually appear" (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading"). Walk checks overload sets when it loads a program (`fortress-repo` skill, `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks"), so its form of a static error is a refusal at load.

### A4. A declaration at the meet whose return type is too wide (slide 4, middle build)

- **Source.** Slide 4 only: beside `m1(x: B, y: C): B` and `m1(x: C, y: B): C`, the disambiguating `m1(x: C, y: C): B` makes the call's run-time type `B` where its static type is `C`, "NOT TYPE-SOUND!".
- **Fortress form.**

      trait B end
      object C extends B end
      m1(x: B, y: C): B = x
      m1(x: C, y: B): C = x
      m1(x: C, y: C): B = y
      run body: c1: C = C; c2: B = C; r: C = m1(c1, c2); println("ran")

  The smallest form of the same defect is `f(x: B): C = C` beside `f(x: C): B = x`.
- **Expected.** A static error on both paths: `m1(C, C)` is more specific than `m1(C, B)`, and its return type `B` is not a subtype of `C`, so no rule makes the pair valid (`advanced/overloading.tex`, "Subtype Rule", paragraph "The Subtype Rule for Functions and Functional Methods").
- **Today.** Compiled: refused, "For m1, the return type of (C, C)->B ... should be a subtype of the return type of (C, B)->C"; the smallest form, "the return type of C->B ... should be a subtype of the return type of B->C". Walk: loads and prints `ran`; the smallest form prints `C`. With `trait C extends B` and `object Co extends C` in place of `object C`, walk refuses: "fails because the first parameter list is a subtype of the second, but the first result is not a subtype of the second".
- **Why walk loads it.** Walk's pair check skips the parameters at which the two lists are equal, and marks the pair excluding when every other parameter of one list is an object type (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:432-433` and `:486`, the team's code at 75be286ac). An object trait type "excludes any type that is not its supertype" (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex`, "Object Trait Types"), and `B` is a supertype of `C`, so the mark is wrong and the return-type condition is never checked. Row 99 records the shortcut's sound use, an object unrelated to the other parameter.
- **Existing tests.** None of a plain pair; the compiled return-type refusals in the tree are of generic declarations (`the return type of Circle->Circle`, `Round->Round`).
- **Test.** New, and a failing one under walk: `tests/XXXReturnRuleObjectParamWalk.fss` with `load_exception_contains=the first result is not a subtype of the second`, under a new row (candidate R1 below). Compiled, new and green: `compiler_tests/XXXReturnRuleMeetCrossing.test` with `compile_err_contains=should be a subtype of the`.

## Group B: rules the revival does differently

### B1. `m2` at `A`, `B` and `C`, valid because `C` is "the only subtype of both" (p. 11:4; slide 6, last build)

- **Source.** §2.1 assumes "class C is the only subtype of both classes A and B" and calls `d21: m2(x: A)`, `d22: m2(x: B)`, `d23: m2(x: C)` valid, `d23` being "the meet of the first two declarations" under the older calculus FF, whose meet is defined among the declarations. Slide 6 adds `m2(x: C): C` the same way.
- **What departs.** Fortress components are open: a later type may extend both `A` and `B`. The revival's Meet Rule asks for a declaration on `A ∩ B`, or for declarations that together cover every value of both, and "it is not necessarily the case that S = (P ∩ Q) since another type may be more specific than both" (`advanced/overloading.tex`, "Meet Rule", and its `revival-meet` callout: "the paper of 2019 has no traits with comprises clauses"). Fortress states the paper's assumption with `comprises` clauses, which FGFV lacks (p. 11:3).
- **Fortress forms and today.**
  - Plain traits `A` and `B`, `object C extends { A, B }`, the three `m2`: refused on both paths, compiled "Invalid overloading of m2 ...: A->String ... and B->String", walk "first parameters x:[B] and x:[A] are unrelated ...". That is the revival's rule.
  - With `trait A comprises { C, Ao }`, `trait B comprises { C, Bo }`, objects `Ao`, `Bo` and `C extends { A, B }`: valid; `m2(a)` for `a: A` holding `C` asserts `"C"`, `m2(Ao)` asserts `"A"`; both paths print `PASS`.
- **Ledger and questions.** None: the text settles it (POSITIONS, "The `comprises` passages read at the level of values (PLAN item 26, row 491)"). `ComprisesMeetCompiled.fss` and `ComprisesMeetWalk.fss` gate the coverage, and the team's `Compiled5.j` the refusal where the listed traits do not exclude.

### B2. `sort` bounded by `A`, `B` and `C`, valid because `C` is the only subtype of both (p. 11:6; slide 7, last build)

- **Source.** §2.2: `d3: sort[P <: C](x: ListI[P])` disambiguates `d1` and `d2` of A6, under §2.1's assumption; the return-type condition for `d1` and `d3` holds because `ListI` is invariant, so each `ListI[X]` has exactly one instance of `d1`.

# The POPL 2019 examples, sorted for the test suite

## In short

- The paper and the talk hold 24 worked examples once the talk's builds that repeat a paper example are folded into it: 11 in group A, 4 in group B, 9 in group C.
- Of the 11 in group A, today's tree fails 4 on one path, and 2 more derived from group B and C examples fail too:
  - walk loads an object that inherits `m(x: Number)` with a body from two unrelated traits (p. 11:2; row 444's family);
  - walk loads `f(x: B): C` beside `f(x: C): B` with `object C extends B`, the talk's "NOT TYPE-SOUND" set (slide 4; a new row);
  - walk loads two generic `sort`s bounded by `A` and by `B` with no declaration at their meet (p. 11:5, slide 7; row 373);
  - the compiled path refuses the talk's opening `add` set, because the compiler prelude's `ZZ32` is an open trait (slide 2; a new row);
  - the paper's `ArrayList`/`List` triple fails on both paths, as its gated expected failures say (p. 11:13; rows 537 and 539);
  - derived: the paper's `sort` set with its meet written `P extends { A, B }` dies compiled (row 537), and the invariant core of the paper's `sort`/`merge` example fails on both paths (p. 11:7; one new compiled row, one walk row optional).
- Group B holds no new question for Pavol. The paper's two sets that rest on "C is the only subtype of both A and B" become valid in Fortress through `comprises` clauses, which the revival's Meet Rule reads as coverage; the union instance of `O.m(3, true)` is his decision for the bound; the No Duplicates wording is row 696.
- Group C waits on the `covariant` keyword (row 404), lower bounds on a method's type parameters, and the static return type carried to run time (phase 5).

## How the examples were run

- Each Fortress form is a test program in the form `tests-writing.md` gives: `component Name`, `export Executable`, the declarations shown, and `run(): () = do ... end` with the body shown. The scratch copies live in the tree's ignored `tmp/` and are not committed.
- Under walk: `bin/fortress walk P.fss`. Compiled: `bin/fortress compile P.fss`, then `bin/fortress run P`. Both with `FORTRESS_CACHES` pointing at a private copy of `default_repository/caches`, so the shared caches took no scratch entry.
- The existing tests named below were run through the harness: `harness-one.sh` on `XXXOverloadExistentialMeetWalk.fss` and `XXXGenericBesidePlainSameDomain.fss` printed `OK (2 tests)`; `junit.sh` with `ONE_JVM=1` on `OverloadExistentialMeetLink.test`, `XXXOverloadExistentialMeet.test`, `XXX2f.test`, `GenericInstanceUnfixedLink.test` and `XXXGenericInstanceUnfixed.test` printed `OK (5 tests)`, each `XXX` file as "Saw expected failure".
- In FGFV a method is called `e.m(e')`; the Fortress forms use top-level functions, which the revival overloads by the same rules (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading"). FGFV's classes become traits, or objects where the example needs a value.
- An overloading that breaks a rule is a static error on both paths: the rules are "checked statically" for the declarations, "whether or not these calls actually appear" (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading"). Walk checks overload sets when it loads a program (`fortress-repo` skill, `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks"), so its form of a static error is a refusal at load.

Written 2026-10-10 at the coordinating session's brief, for the coordinating session, which plans the next batch, and for the curator, Pavol. Every Fortress form below was run under walk and through the compiled path on the tree at 75be286ac (built, caches kept); nothing in the original tree was edited, and no ledger row was opened. Page numbers are the paper's (11:1 to 11:28); slide numbers are the talk's. -->
2	
3	# The POPL 2019 examples, sorted for the test suite
4	
5	## In short
6	
7	- The paper and the talk hold 24 worked examples once the talk's builds that repeat a paper example are folded into it: 11 in group A, 4 in group B, 9 in group C.
8	- Of the 11 in group A, today's tree fails 5: four on one path, and one on both, as its gated tests expect. Two tests derived from group B and C examples fail too:
9	  - walk loads an object that inherits `m(x: Number)` with a body from two unrelated traits (p. 11:2; row 444's family);
10	  - walk loads `f(x: B): C` beside `f(x: C): B` with `object C extends B`, the talk's "NOT TYPE-SOUND" set (slide 4; a new row);
11	  - walk loads two generic `sort`s bounded by `A` and by `B` with no declaration at their meet (p. 11:5, slide 7; row 373);
12	  - the compiled path refuses the talk's opening `add` set, because the compiler prelude's `ZZ32` is an open trait (slide 2; a new row);
13	  - the paper's `ArrayList`/`List` triple fails on both paths, as its gated expected failures say (p. 11:13; rows 537 and 539);
14	  - derived: the paper's `sort` set with its meet written `P extends { A, B }` dies compiled (row 537), and the invariant core of the paper's `sort`/`merge` example fails on both paths (p. 11:7; one new compiled row, one walk row optional).
15	- Group B holds no new question for Pavol. The paper's two sets that rest on "C is the only subtype of both A and B" become valid in Fortress through `comprises` clauses, which the revival's Meet Rule reads as coverage; the union instance of `O.m(3, true)` is his decision for the bound; the No Duplicates wording is row 696.
16	- Group C waits on the `covariant` keyword (row 404), lower bounds on a method's type parameters, and the static return type carried to run time (phase 5).
17	
18	## How the examples were run
19	
20	- Each Fortress form is a test program in the form `tests-writing.md` gives: `component Name`, `export Executable`, the declarations shown, and `run(): () = do ... end` with the body shown. The scratch copies live in the tree's ignored `tmp/` and are not committed.
21	- Under walk: `bin/fortress walk P.fss`. Compiled: `bin/fortress compile P.fss`, then `bin/fortress run P`. Both with `FORTRESS_CACHES` pointing at a private copy of `default_repository/caches`, so the shared caches took no scratch entry.
22	- The existing tests named below were run through the harness: `harness-one.sh` on `XXXOverloadExistentialMeetWalk.fss` and `XXXGenericBesidePlainSameDomain.fss` printed `OK (2 tests)`; `junit.sh` with `ONE_JVM=1` on `OverloadExistentialMeetLink.test`, `XXXOverloadExistentialMeet.test`, `XXX2f.test`, `GenericInstanceUnfixedLink.test` and `XXXGenericInstanceUnfixed.test` printed `OK (5 tests)`, each `XXX` file as "Saw expected failure".
23	- In FGFV a method is called `e.m(e')`; the Fortress forms use top-level functions, which the revival overloads by the same rules (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading"). FGFV's classes become traits, or objects where the example needs a value.
24	- An overloading that breaks a rule is a static error on both paths: the rules are "checked statically" for the declarations, "whether or not these calls actually appear" (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading"). Walk checks overload sets when it loads a program (`fortress-repo` skill, `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks"), so its form of a static error is a refusal at load.
25	
26	## Group A: rules the revival implements
27	
28	### A1. Two traits each give `m(x: Number)` a body; an object extends both (p. 11:2)
29	
30	- **Source.** §1: classes `A` and `B` each declare `m` at `Number`, `C` extends both, and `c.m(0)` is ambiguous, "because neither A nor B is more specific than each other".
31	- **Fortress form.**
32	
33	      trait A  m(x: Number): ZZ32 = 1  end
34	      trait B  m(x: Number): ZZ32 = 2  end
35	      object C extends { A, B } end
36	      run body: println(C.m(0))
37	
38	- **Expected.** A static error on both paths. `C` provides both dotted methods, `(A, Number)` and `(B, Number)` are neither ordered nor incompatible, and `C` provides no declaration at their meet (`advanced/overloading.tex`, "Meet Rule", paragraph "The Meet Rule for Dotted Methods").
39	- **Today.** Compiled: refused, "Invalid overloading of m in trait C: (A, Number)->ZZ32 ... and (B, Number)->ZZ32". Walk: loads and prints `1`. With `trait C extends { A, B }` and an object below it, walk prints `1` too.
40	- **Existing tests.** Walk: `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXDottedMethodMeetInheritedWalk.fss`, the diamond with one abstract and one concrete `g` (row 444's diamond shape). Compiled: none of this shape; the functional-method diamonds `XXXFunctionalMethodMeetSelfSecondNoMeet` and `XXXFunctionalMethodMeetInheritedFromApi` are its siblings.
41	- **Test.** New, and a failing one under walk: `tests/XXXDottedMethodMeetBothBodiesWalk.fss` with a `.test` file, `load_exception_contains=Invalid overloading of m`, recorded under row 444. Compiled, new and green: `compiler_tests/XXXDottedMethodMeetBothBodies.test`, `compile` with `compile_err_contains=Invalid overloading of m in`.
42	
43	### A2. `m1` at `(B, C)` beside `m1` at `(C, B)`, with `C` below `B` (p. 11:4; slide 4, first build; slide 3, the three-declaration build)
44	
45	- **Source.** §2.1: `m1(x: B, y: C): B` and `m1(x: C, y: B): B`; `m1(c, c)` is ambiguous "due to symmetric multiple dispatch". Slide 4 returns `C` from the second; slide 3 has the same crossing pair as `add` over `List` and `SortedList`, beside `add(List, List)`.
46	- **Fortress form.**

49	      object C extends B end
50	      m1(x: B, y: C): B = x
51	      m1(x: C, y: B): B = y
52	      run body: println(m1(C, C))
53	
54	- **Expected.** A static error on both paths: neither parameter type is a subtype of the other, they do not exclude, and no declaration is at `(B, C) ∩ (C, B)`, which is `(C, C)` (`advanced/overloading.tex`, "Meet Rule", paragraph "The Meet Rule for Functions").
55	- **Today.** Both refuse. Compiled: "Invalid overloading of m1 in component ...: (B, C)->B ... and (C, B)->B". Walk: "Overloading of ... m1(x:C,y:B):B ... and ... m1(x:B,y:C):B ... fails because (first) x is more specific than (second) x but (first) y is less specific than (second) y". Slide 3's `add` set without its fourth declaration gives the same two refusals.
56	- **Existing tests.** Compiled: the team's `compiler_tests/Compiled2.f.fss` through `XXX2f.test`, `f(x: O, y: T)` beside `f(x: T, y: O)`, refused today. Walk: none of this shape.

60	
61	- **Source.** §2.1: `m2(x: A): Boolean` and `m2(x: B): Boolean`; `m2(c)` is ambiguous "due to multiple inheritance". Slide 6 returns `C` from both.
62	- **Fortress form.**

export Executable
(* This test should fail because of crossed overloading. *)
trait T end
trait S extends T end
a(s:S, t:T)=do
  println("a1 called")
end
a(t:T, s:S)=do
  println("a2 called")
end
run():()=do
  println("fail") (* TEST SHOULD NOT RUN *)
end
end

component XXXInheritedOverload
export Executable
trait Base
end
trait Sub1 extends Base excludes {Sub2}
end
trait Sub2 extends Base excludes {Sub1}
end
trait T1
  a(x:Sub1, y:Base):ZZ32 = 2
end
trait T2
  a(x:Base, y:Sub2):ZZ32 = 1
end
object O() extends {T1, T2}
end

component XXXGenericOverload
export Executable
(* Should not compile *)
(* This demonstrates why it is not correct to
   substitute bounds for generic type parameters
   when checking correctness of overlaoding. *)
trait B  end
trait A extends B end
f[\ U extends A, V extends B \] ( x:U, y:V) = 1
f[\ U extends A, V extends B \] ( x:V, y:U) = 2
f[\ U extends A, V extends B \] ( x:U, y:U) = 3
run():() = do
  println("FAIL: should have failed in generic overloading of f" )
end
end

input.message:
Commit: fa9a32e39 adds `explorations/reviews/popl2019-examples.md` and nothing else. It is not pushed.

I ran every example's Fortress form under walk and through the compiled path, on the tree at 75be286ac, which builds clean and kept its caches. I also ran the existing tests I name through the harness: `harness-one.sh` printed OK (2 tests) and `junit.sh` printed OK (5 tests), every `XXX` test as an expected failure.

**Counts.** The paper and talk hold 24 worked examples once the talk builds that repeat a paper example are folded in.
- Group A: 11.
- Group B: 4.
- Group C: 9.
- Two tests derived from a group B and a group C example also test rules the revival implements.

**Examples today's tree fails:**
- A1 (p. 11:2): two traits each give `m(x: Number)` a body, and an object extends both. Walk loads it and prints 1; the compiled checker refuses it. This is row 444's family.
- A4 (slide 4): `f(x: B): C` beside `f(x: C): B`, with `object C extends B`. Walk loads and runs it; the compiled checker refuses it. Walk's overload check marks the pair as excluding when the other parameters are object types (`OverloadedFunction.java:427-433, :486`). This is a new defect.
- A6 (p. 11:5, slide 7): `sort[\P extends A\]` beside `sort[\P extends B\]` over `ListI[\P\]`, with no declaration at their meet. Walk loads and runs it; the compiled checker refuses it. Row 373.
- A10 (slide 2): `add(ZZ32, ZZ32)` beside `add(List, List)`. The compiled path refuses it because the compiler prelude's `ZZ32` is an open trait; walk runs it. This is a new defect, and the switch-over removes it.
- A8 (p. 11:13): the `ArrayList`/`List` triple fails on both paths. Its existing expected-failure tests already record this (rows 537 and 539).
- A-B2, derived (p. 11:6): the paper's `sort` set with its meet written `R extends { A, B }`. Walk passes. Compiled, the compile stops with "duplicate entry" when all three parameters are named `P`; with `P`, `Q` and `R` the run dies with "Unable to read serialized data". Row 537.
- A-C4, derived (p. 11:7): the paper's `sort`/`merge` example rewritten without variance (a type parameter only the return type mentions).
  - Compiled: the program compiles, then the run dies at class load with "VerifyError: Bad return type" in the generated `sort` dispatcher. This is a new defect, related to rows 496 and 538.
  - Walk: it gives `Sorted[\Any\]`, and `merge` then fails with a "Unification error". The specification's callout already describes this walk limit, but no ledger row tracks it.

**Candidate ledger rows.** Each new row passes `ledger.py check --rows` except for its `?` number; the note holds their full text.
- R1, new (walk, section 4): walk's overload check marks a pair as excluding through an object-type parameter even when that object extends the other parameter's type.
- R2, new (prelude, section 5): the prelude's `trait ZZ32` has no `comprises` clause, so the compiled path refuses `add(ZZ32, ZZ32)` beside `add(List, List)`.
- R3, new (codegen, section 5): a dispatched generic declaration whose type parameter only the return type mentions fails JVM verification. If you count it as row 538's issue, make it a note there.
- R4, optional (walk, design limit, section 4): walk runs such a declaration at its bound instead of at the call's static type.
- Note on row 444: the paper's two-bodies diamond shape.
- Note on row 373: two reproducers it lacks, the `sort` pair from A6 and the duplicate pair `dup[\T\](Box[\T\])` / `dup[\U\](Box[\U\])`.
- Note on row 696: the compiled checker already refuses an equivalent pair ("There are multiple declarations of dup with the same parameter type"), so only the specification's wording is wrong.
- Note on row 537: two more shapes, the meet written with two bounds and the `comprises` form of the paper's `sort` set.

**Group B.** None of the four needs a question for Pavol.
- B1 and B2: the paper's `m2` and `sort` sets are valid only because "C is the only subtype of both A and B". The revival needs `comprises` clauses to say that.
  - With them, the checker accepts both sets, and the `m2` form passes on both paths.
  - The compiled run of the `sort` form dies (row 537). Walk wrongly accepts the plain-trait form of `sort` (row 373).
- B3: for `O.m(3, true)` the revival takes the bound `Any` instead of the paper's union, as Pavol decided. Written without a bound, the compiled path hits row 412.
- B4: the No Duplicates wording is row 696.

**Group C.** These wait on the `covariant` and `contravariant` keywords (row 404), on lower bounds for a method's type parameters (`where` clauses, row 677), and on the static return type reaching the compiled dispatcher (phase 5).

**Test rung.**
- Seven tests fail today. One of them waits on R4, and one (the row-537 pair) is optional.
- Seven new tests pass today.
- A2 is already gated by the team's `XXX2f.test` and `XXXoverloadTest5.fss`.

**What I could not do.** I did not add the note's line to `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`, because the brief allowed only the note. The line it owes:
- `explorations/reviews/popl2019-examples.md`: The worked examples of Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, "Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance", POPL 2019, and of Gyunghee Park's talk on it, sorted into what each can do for the test suite.

I did not trace whether the compiled checker accepts the `comprises` form of the `sort` set through its coverage check or through its reading of the `comprises` clauses.
